title: Speculative Coupled Decoding for Autoregressive Visual Generation
one_liner: Speculative Coupled Decoding guesses multiple image tokens at once by predicting what the model might choose next, then accepting the guesses that are actually correct, so one forward pass generates several tokens instead of one.
lead: Autoregressive visual generation (building images one piece at a time, like writing one letter at a time) is impractical because it needs thousands of forward passes to make a single image. This paper shows that you can guess multiple pieces for the next step, run the model just once to check which guesses are right, accept the correct ones, and reject the wrong ones — trading a tiny bit of guessing overhead for a big reduction in the actual model runs needed. The trick: make your guesses in a way that agrees with itself across iterations, so more guesses get accepted.

paras: An autoregressive model (a model that generates one piece at a time, like writing a letter-by-letter sentence) must run the full neural network once per piece it wants to make. Generating a 256 by 256 pixel image in pieces means 65536 forward passes. Running 65536 passes takes hours on a single GPU.

A naive speedup attempt: guess the next 4 pieces (image pieces or chunks) without running the model, then run the model once to check if any of your guesses were right, and keep the ones that match. But if you guess independently each time (like rolling a die separately for each guess), the guesses rarely match what the model actually picks. You end up accepting maybe 1 out of 4, and you wasted 3 guesses, so the speedup is only 25 percent at best.

callout.html: SCD generates multiple tokens by guessing what the model will choose next (using an iterative technique that tends to agree with itself), so that more guesses match the model's actual picks, and you accept more of them per forward pass.

panels.title: 1. The problem: one token per pass

steps.text: Use a mathematical trick (Jacobi iteration) to generate a batch of 4 candidate tokens all at once, without running the model.
Modify the guessing process so candidates tend to be the same across iterations, maximizing agreement without slowing down.
Feed all candidates into the real model in a single forward pass.
Check which candidates the model actually picks. Keep the matches, discard the misses.
Use the accepted tokens, iterate. If some candidates were rejected, re-guess and re-check those positions.

object.h2: What the paper changes: draft token generation
paras: The paper modifies the sampling process (how you pick a candidate token when you do not know what the real model wants). Instead of independent random guesses, it makes guesses that are statistically dependent, tuned to agree with each other.

hidden.name: coupling probability
paras: The coupling probability is how often your guesses produce the same token across successive iterations. If you guess token A on step 1 and token A again on step 2, that is a coupling event. Without coupling, two independent guesses match maybe 5% of the time (by random luck, if there are 20 possible tokens). With coupling, you can push that to 50%, 70%, even higher.
The paper maximizes this probability by adjusting how the Jacobi iteration works. Higher coupling means more guesses get accepted when the model runs, so fewer actual forward passes are needed.

heat.caption: Darker colors show higher agreement (coupling) between guesses. Before coupling: mostly different. After: many same token.

reads.html: Coupling is just making your guesses tend to pick the same token, so when you check them all against the real model, more of them turn out correct.

The paper maximizes the mutual information between successive draft samples using information-theoretic bounds, ensuring that the probability of sampling identical tokens is as high as possible while maintaining the lossless property.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: how coupling reduces forward passes
paras: Jacobi iteration is a numerical technique that starts with a rough guess and refines it by running the same calculation multiple times. Each refinement pulls the guess closer to the true answer. Here, each refinement is a forward pass estimate of what token the model wants next.

Without coupling, each iteration samples its candidate independently. The problem: the model learns a specific, peaked distribution over the next token (e.g., 60% token A, 30% token B, 10% token C). A random sample from that distribution is token A roughly 60% of the time. On iteration 1, you might get A. On iteration 2, the model has not changed, but your independent sample might give B. You waste a draft slot. With coupling, you modify the sampling to preferentially pick the same token again, so by iteration 3, you still have A as your guess, and when you finally run the model, A is correct. The model only changed positions where you guessed wrong, not positions where you guessed right repeatedly. This is an information-theoretic change: you are deliberately reducing the entropy (randomness) of your guesses.

The speedup comes purely from acceptance rate. If 75% of your guesses get accepted (instead of 25%), and you guess 4 tokens per pass, then you accept 3 tokens per pass instead of 1. You need only one-third as many forward passes.

stages.s: Run model once on all candidates
Accept candidates that match the model

math.h2: The equation: expected speedup from coupling
math.words: speedup equals one divided by the fraction of candidates that get accepted
symbols: how many tokens you guess per forward pass, e.g., 4
fraction of guesses that match the model, e.g., 0.75
batch_size minus 1, accounting for the baseline forward pass

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Without coupling: acceptance_rate = 0.25 (only 1 out of 4 guesses correct). speedup = 4 / (1 + (1 - 0.25) * 3) = 4 / (1 + 2.25) = 4 / 3.25 = 1.23×. Barely faster.
With coupling: acceptance_rate = 0.75 (three out of 4 guesses correct). speedup = 4 / (1 + (1 - 0.75) * 3) = 4 / (1 + 0.75) = 4 / 1.75 = 2.29×. Much better.
With even stronger coupling: acceptance_rate = 0.95 (almost all guesses correct). speedup = 4 / (1 + (1 - 0.95) * 3) = 4 / (1 + 0.15) = 4 / 1.15 = 3.48×. Close to the batch-size limit.

math.note: The equation shows that coupling, by raising acceptance rate, compresses the denominator, making the speedup grow.

bars.h2: Quality and speed with and without coupling

charts.title: Independent guessing (baseline SD)
charts.note: Most guesses do not match the model (only one out of four guesses is right on average), so you accept almost none, so speedup is tiny.

charts.title: Speculative Coupled Decoding
charts.note: Coupling steers all guess iterations to favor the same piece, raising acceptance from 25 percent to 75 percent. Three accepted pieces per pass cuts total forward passes by two-thirds. Same quality (acceptance test ensures every kept guess is right).

items.b: Coupling breaks if the model's distribution is too flat.
items.html: If the next token has nearly equal probability across many choices (uniform distribution, not peaked), coupling cannot push all guesses to the same token. Acceptance rates drop. The speedup falls. The method works best when the model is confident (peaked distributions).

items.b: Too many rejected guesses waste computation.
items.html: If coupling is weak or the model is uncertain, you may accept only 1 out of 4 guesses, defeating the speedup entirely. The paper assumes at least a 2 times acceptance rate for four-piece batches to be worth it.

items.b: Coupling overhead could be higher than expected in some architectures.
items.html: The coupling modification is a single line of code, but if the underlying Jacobi iteration is implemented inefficiently, the per-iteration cost could spike, reducing the net speedup.

items.b: Done right, the method is lossless.
items.html: The paper proves that the final image is identical to the output of standard autoregressive generation: no quality loss, only speed gain. The acceptance check is exact.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should generate a 64 by 64 or 128 by 128 pixel RGB image using an autoregressive visual model. Measure the acceptance rate (fraction of guesses that match the model). Show that with coupling, the acceptance rate rises from around 20 percent (baseline speculative decoding) to around 50 percent or higher, because coupling makes repeated guesses stay aligned, so more match what the model actually picks. Run the full generation with and without coupling, and show that the wall-clock time is the same or faster with coupling (because fewer model forward passes are needed), and the image quality is identical to standard generation (because the acceptance check ensures only correct guesses are kept).
demo.metric_eq: wall_clock_time_standard / wall_clock_time_coupled, and acceptance_rate = accepted_tokens / (batch_size * num_iterations)
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that coupling trades almost no overhead for a dramatic rise in acceptance rate, and that this rise directly shrinks the number of model forward passes needed.
